General organisation of CAPL-2 field measurements

All CAPL-2 tests and measurements were administered by a team of 35 sport science students trained to ensure consistency and objectivity in test administration and scoring. All questionnaire and physical test data were collected over four half-days. Questionnaires were administered in classrooms or in dedicated quiet areas conducive to concentration, in groups of approximately 10 students, while physical tests were conducted on sports fields, playgrounds, and in gymnasiums. All data were collected between March and May 2024.

Characterisation of movement behaviour distributions

The characterization of movement behaviour distributions consisted of describing activity intensity distribution and patterns of sedentary time accumulation. Activity intensity distribution was quantified using the intensity gradient (Rowlands et al., 2018), while sedentary accumulation patterns were characterised using the power-law exponent alpha (Chastin & Granat, 2010). These metrics were computed for participants with at least four valid days.

The intensity gradient describes the distribution of time across the full spectrum of activity intensities over a given day of the monitoring period. It corresponds to the slope of the regression line between the logarithm of accumulated time spent in a given intensity bin and the logarithm of the midpoint of that intensity bin (Rowlands et al., 2018). Because accumulated time decreases as intensity increases, the intensity gradient is always negative (Backes et al., 2022). Consequently, more negative values indicate lower accumulation of time at higher intensities. The intensity gradient was computed for each valid day using raw acceleration data as originally proposed (Rowlands et al., 2018), that is, using the ENMO (Euclidean Norm Minus One) metric averaged over 5-s epochs, and intensity bins of 25 mg resolution (0-25, 25-50, 50-75, … 4000, >4000). Computations were performed using {GGIR} package algorithms (Migueles et al., 2019). Daily average of intensity gradient was then computed for statistical analysis.

The power-law exponent alpha was computed from all sedentary bouts recorded during valid days, as described by Chastin et Granat (2010). A lower alpha value reflects a sedentary accumulation pattern characterised by a higher proportion of longer bouts (Backes et al., 2022). A sedentary bout was defined as any sequence of at least one 15-second epoch with fewer than 45 counts per 15 seconds (Hänggi et al., 2013). Calculations were performed using algorithms implemented in the {activAnalyzer} R package ( de Müllenheim, 2025b).

Statistical analysis

All data processing and statistical analyses were performed using R programming language v4.6.1 (R Core Team, 2024) and the RStudio environment (v2026.08.2: "Yellow Yarrow"). In the results section, descriptive statistics for continuous variables are reported as medians (25th-75th percentile), as distributions were generally non-Gaussian. Categorical variables are reported as counts and percentages.

Comparisons of CAPL-2 scores between sexes

Girls and boys were compared using three complementary approaches: (i) the CAPL-2 total score (single outcome); (ii) all CAPL-2 domain scores simultaneously (four outcomes: physical competence, daily behaviour, motivation and confidence, and knowledge and understanding); and (iii) all CAPL-2 item scores simultaneously (18 outcomes, e.g., PACER, CAMSA, etc.).

For all approaches, between-sex comparisons were conducted using nonparametric procedures assessing stochastic equality and providing relative effects (stochastic superiority). Specifically, for univariate comparisons of physical literacy scores, the Brunner-Munzel test was used. The relative effect corresponds to the probability that a randomly selected individual from one group (e.g., boys) has a higher score than a randomly selected individual from the other group (e.g., girls). For multivariate comparisons of CAPL-2 domains and items, nonparametric multivariate analyses were performed (W. W. Burchett et al., 2017). In this context, relative effects represent, for a given outcome, the probability that an individual randomly selected from one group (e.g., girls) has a higher value than an individual drawn from the combined sample of both groups.

Because the objective was to compare the full outcome distributions rather than central tendencies, and because outcome distributions were generally heterogeneous, measures of central tendency were considered inappropriate for group comparisons. In contrast, relative effects combined with nonparametric methods were considered more robust and appropriate, particularly when analysing mixed outcome types (e.g., continuous variables and discrete variables with limited response levels) as justified in W. W. Burchett et al. (2017).

Comparisons of movement behaviour distribution metrics across physical literacy profiles

Physical literacy profiles were compared using nonparametric multivariate analyses (W. W. Burchett et al., 2017), as described above. Analyses included participants with at least four valid accelerometer days and a valid CAPL-2 profile. Unlike the previous analyses, no imputation of an additional valid day was performed.

Statistical significance

A sex difference in CAPL-2 total score was considered significant when the p-value associated with the Brunner-Munzel test (t-approximation) was ≤ 0.05. Sex differences in CAPL-2 domain and item scores, as well as differences in movement behaviour distribution metrics across physical literacy profiles, were considered significant when the p-value associated with the ANOVA-type statistic (F-approximation) was ≤ 0.05. When a significant overall multivariate effect was detected, multiple comparisons were performed to determine for which combinations of outcomes significant differences between groups existed, again using the ANOVA-type statistic (F-approximation), while controlling the family-wise error rate at 5%. Analyses were performed using complete cases as generally required for nonparametric methods (W. W. Burchett et al., 2017). No imputation of missing data was performed.

As this is an exploratory study, the statistical procedures described above should be interpreted as tools to identify or update prior assumptions regarding potentially relevant research directions, rather than to support confirmatory scientific claims (Ditroilo et al., 2025).

Accordingly, procedures controlling the family-wise error rate should be viewed as methods for more robust pattern detection to guide future hypothesis-driven studies, rather than as a basis for inferential claims.

Reproducibility materials

Data processing, data integration, and statistical analyses were implemented in a reproducible pipeline using R. Instructions and materials for running the pipeline are available in a Zenodo repository (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24053778).

RESULTS

Global descriptive analysis

Among the 99 children included in the study (53 girls [54%]; mean age 10.3 ± 0.5 years), 71 (39 girls [55%]) completed all CAPL-2 measurements with valid results allowing computation of the total physical literacy score (overall completion rate = 72%). The CAPL-2 scores for all participants and by sex are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. As shown in Figure 1, regarding the physical competence domain, two children could not obtain a physical competence score (overall completion rate = 98%): one girl did not complete any of the physical tests, and one girl did not complete the PACER test. Regarding the daily behaviour domain, 27 children could not obtain a daily behaviour score (overall completion rate = 73%): one girl did not complete the accelerometer measurement, and the remaining children did not obtain enough valid days of accelerometer measurement. All 99 children successfully completed the measurements from the remaining CAPL-2 domains. Finally, a total of 47 participants (23 girls [49%]) had both a valid CAPL-2 profile and at least four valid days of accelerometer wear. Among these, 4 (9%) participants were classified as "Beginning", 14 (30%) as "Progressing", 9 (19%) as "Achieving", and 20 (43%) as "Excelling".

Comparisons of CAPL-2 scores between sexes

The relative effects depicting the differences in CAPL-2 scores between sexes are shown in Table 1. The multivariate combinations of CAPL-2 domain and item scores for which girls and boys differed significantly are shown in Figure 2 and Supplemental Material 1 (see https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24053778), respectively.

From a descriptive perspective, boys were stochastically superior to girls for the total physical literacy score (relative effect = 0.71) as well as for all domain scores (relative effects between 0.61 and 0.69) except knowledge and understanding (relative effect = 0.44). Regarding item scores, boys were also stochastically superior to girls for most scores (relative effects between 0.52 and 0.69), excluding knowledge and understanding of physical activity, cardiorespiratory fitness, and sport skill improvement (relative effects between 0.37 and 0.48). The relative effect was highest for the total physical literacy score, close to the maximum theoretical relative effect.

During exploratory testing analyses, we found a significant sex difference for the total physical literacy score (t(69) = 3.29, p = 0.002), the multivariate combination of domain scores (F(3.55, 242.06) = 3.99, p = 0.005), and the multivariate combination of item scores (F(8.42, 575.14) = 3.65, p < 0.001). The domain score combinations for which the sexes differed significantly were those including the motivation and confidence score, including the motivation and confidence score alone. Several combinations of item scores differed significantly between sexes. The significant combinations of item scores involving the fewest items included at least six of the following: PACER shuttle run, average daily step count, self-reported number of days with MVPA, intrinsic motivation, perceived competence for physical activity, perceived adequacy for physical activity, cardiorespiratory fitness definition, physical activity comprehension and understanding, and sport skill improvement knowledge. This series of items should be viewed as the minimum combination of items to be taken together to consider girls and boys as different and on which efforts should be made to promote sex equality in terms of physical literacy.

Comparison of movement behaviour distribution metrics across physical literacy profiles

The relative effects depicting the differences in movement behaviour distribution metrics across physical literacy profiles are shown in Table 2, the distributions of the corresponding variables are shown in Figure 3, and the multivariate combinations of movement behaviour metrics for which physical literacy profiles differed significantly are shown in Figure 4.

From a descriptive perspective, regarding the intensity gradient, the two highest physical literacy profiles ("Achieving" and "Excelling") had relative effects higher than 0.50 and were stochastically superior to the "Progressing" profile (relative effect of 0.40) and to the "Beginning" profile (relative effect of 0.18). These results indicate that, in this sample, a higher physical literacy profile was associated with a greater tendency to spend time in higher activity intensity bins. Regarding the power-law exponent alpha related to sedentary behaviour, relative effects were more balanced across physical literacy profiles, with the two middle profiles ("Progressing" and "Achieving") being close and having the highest relative effects (0.55 and 0.57, respectively), followed by the "Excelling" profile and finally the "Beginning" profile, with relative effects of 0.45 and 0.39 respectively. Thus, the hierarchy of physical literacy profiles was less clearly reflected in power-law exponent alpha related to sedentary behaviour than in the intensity gradient. However, the "Beginning" profile stood out from the other profiles due to its stochastic inferiority for both the intensity gradient and power-law exponent alpha.

During exploratory testing analyses, we found a significant difference for the multivariate combination of movement behaviour distribution metrics (F(5.56, 50.40) = 2.46, p = 0.040). The metric combinations for which physical literacy profiles differed significantly included the intensity gradient alone and the combination of both the intensity gradient and the power-law exponent alpha to sedentary behaviour.

DISCUSSION

The present study consisted of two exploratory analyses related to the concept of physical literacy in late childhood: (i) comparing CAPL-2 scores between sexes, and (ii) comparing movement behaviour distribution metrics across physical literacy profiles. These analyses were exploratory in nature, as they were conducted a posteriori following data collection initially performed to inform the urban and social policies of the city of Avrillé, France.

The recruited sample showed relatively good results for overall physical literacy and its domains, with scores being nearly systematically higher than estimates from large cohorts in other countries (Hadier et al., 2024; Kaioglou et al., 2020; Longmuir et al., 2015). In particular, the sample performed especially well in the physical competence domain, both in absolute scores and relative to other cohorts, as well as in knowledge and understanding of physical activity, while showing results around the average for the daily behaviour domain. Of note, despite the non-negligible loss of participants in the analysis of total physical literacy score due to missing data for the average daily step count item, the completion rate in the present study (72% for total physical literacy score) remains satisfactory compared with other studies reporting overall completion rates of 52% to 100% for total physical literacy score (Hadier et al., 2024; Kaioglou et al., 2020; Longmuir et al., 2015).

Regarding movement behaviour distribution, our sample had a median intensity gradient of -2.2, which was similar to estimates obtained in previous studies, with values around -2.0 to -2.3 (e.g., Fairclough et al., 2023 Fairclough et al., , 2025;; Janda et al., 2023; Taj et al., 2026). However, our estimate may not be directly comparable with those from previous studies due to differences in the methods used to compute the intensity gradient (hip vs. wrist). Moreover, the median power-law exponent alpha for sedentary behaviour (2.2) was slightly above the 5th-95th percentile range (1.6-2.1) observed in a large cohort of Hispanic/Latino youth aged 8 to 16 years (Carlson et al., 2023), suggesting a relatively high level of fragmentation of sedentary time in the children of the present study. However, a precise comparison remains difficult due to differences in the accelerometer used (ActiGraph vs Actical) and the minimum duration of a bout (≥15 s vs ≥60 s).

Comparisons of CAPL-2 scores between sexes

The highest relative effects observed in our sample, depicting tendencies for boys to be superior to girls in total physical literacy score as well as in the physical competence, daily behaviour, and motivation and confidence domains, are consistent with results from large studies conducted in other countries such as Greece (Kaioglou et al., 2020), Pakistan (Hadier et al., 2024), and Canada (Longmuir et al., 2015). However, the hierarchy of domains in terms of effect magnitude may differ and comparisons are ultimately difficult to establish, as the effects used in the present study were rank-based, which was not the case in previous studies.

The significant between-sex differences observed for the total physical literacy score and the combinations of domain scores including the motivation and confidence score encourage conducting confirmatory studies focusing primarily on sex differences in overall physical literacy score and the motivation and confidence domain score in French children living in a sociodemographic context similar to that encountered in the present study: a city in the top tertile of French cities ranked by median household income (Insee, 2010). Along these lines, such an investigation could also consider testing differences primarily for intrinsic motivation, perceived competence, and perceived adequacy in relation to physical activity, as suggested by the combinations of item scores for which girls and boys significantly differed. Of note, in our sample, based on the values of the relative effects, other CAPL-2 domain and item scores may also deserve attention in future confirmatory studies, particularly the physical competence domain along with the PACER test (relative effects of 0.64 and 0.68, respectively), and the daily behaviour domain along with the self-reported number of days with MVPA (relative effects of 0.61 and 0.67, respectively). Confirming the identified differences could inform urban and social policies aimed at promoting healthy movement behaviours based on the physical literacy framework, particularly targeting girls if the direction of the sex difference were confirmed.

Comparison of movement behaviour distribution metrics across physical literacy profiles

To our knowledge, the present study is the first to investigate associations between physical literacy profiles and movement behaviour distribution metrics in children. This kind of investigation aims at questioning the extent to which the concept of physical literacy is coherent with what it is intended to predict, that is, a given activity style. One particularity of the CAPL-2, the physical literacy framework used here, is that it already includes a physical activity behaviour component. While such a component can be justified by the fact that the assessment of actual movement behaviours at a given point in time may reflect physical activity habits and therefore the likelihood of being and remaining active over time, which is a core aspect theoretically predicted by the physical literacy concept, its raises potential tautological issues when analysing associations between physical literacy and movement behaviours (Cornish et al., 2020). Interestingly, the movement behaviour metrics used in the CAPL-2 (average daily step count and number of days with MVPA), more precisely in the daily behaviour domain, are essentially indicators of physical activity volume (Keadle et al., 2017).

In that sense, the CAPL-2 is based on an incomplete picture of the physical activity profile, which should be described using both total physical activity and the distribution of activity intensity throughout the day, the latter being captured by the intensity gradient (Rowlands et al., 2018). Thus, our analysis of the intensity gradient aimed at exploring whether the hierarchy of physical literacy profiles reflects the likelihood of accumulating time at higher intensities, which is emerging as an independent predictor of health indicators in children (Backes et al., 2022). Of note, in the present study, the intensity gradient was only moderately correlated with the total step count in children having four valid days and a complete CAPL-2 profile (r = 0.44), confirming its relative independence from the daily behaviour component of the CAPL-2.

Based on a similar rationale as for the intensity gradient, metrics describing sedentary accumulation patterns were also worth considering for investigating associations between physical literacy and movement behaviours, since no measurement of sedentary behaviour is included within the physical literacy assessment framework. However, we chose to focus on a metric describing the pattern of sedentary time accumulation rather than total sedentary time, since it was deemed that total sedentary time could already be partly and indirectly captured by the intensity gradient. Moreover, the pattern of sedentary time accumulation has also been considered as relevant based on its association with health outcomes in youth (Carlson et al., 2023). While several metrics other than the power-law exponent alpha could have been used to describe in the present study sedentary accumulation patterns (Backes et al., 2022), the power-law exponent alpha was, by construction, the most general (because it describes the shape of the whole distribution of sedentary bouts durations) and therefore the most appropriate from a theoretical perspective. Interestingly, in the present study, the power-law exponent alpha was weakly correlated with step count (r = 0.16) and the intensity gradient (r = 0.15) in children having four valid days and a complete CAPL-2 profile, confirming its usefulness for describing movement behaviour profiles.

The significant multivariate effect of physical literacy profile on movement behaviour metrics observed during exploratory testing, primarily driven by a difference in the intensity gradient, encourages conducting confirmatory studies to validate a distinction between physical literacy profiles for the intensity gradient. If confirmed, this would indicate that the more physically literate children are, the more likely they are to distribute their activity time towards higher intensities, possibly in a regular manner throughout their daily routines (Whitehead, 2010). In contrast, in our sample, there was a lack of close correspondence between the hierarchy of physical literacy profiles and the power-law exponent alpha related to sedentary behaviour, indicating that these profiles did not adequately reflect the patterns of bout durations with which sedentary time is accumulated. If confirmed in future studies, this lack of correspondence between the profiles and sedentary accumulation patterns could be worth considering when designing interventions aimed at promoting healthy movement behaviours, since it would mean that the physical literacy assessment framework has difficulty capturing information that is potentially relevant from a public health perspective, as the fragmentation of sedentary behaviour is associated with distinct metabolic outcomes independently of overall physical activity levels (Carlson et al., 2023).

Limitations

The present exploratory study has several limitations. First, we had no information on the sociodemographic characteristics of the participants (e.g., parental socioeconomic status, household income), other than sex and age. Future studies should consider including such information to control for potential sources of bias when comparing sexes for a given CAPL-2 score. That said, additional descriptive analyses (see sections 7 and 8 from the HTML report of the project's analytical pipeline: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24053778) revealed that the distribution of participants with complete and incomplete data within each recruitment school was similar for girls and boys. Moreover, all recruitment schools except one (which contributed only two participants) had a relatively high Social Position Index (115 to 140 on a scale of 45 to 185, calculated by the French Ministry of National Education from parents' socioprofessional categories). This suggests that socioeconomic profile is unlikely to have substantially confounded our results. Second, we observed comprehension difficulties among some children, particularly for items related to the affective domain of physical literacy, presented in a structured alternative response format (Harter, 1985). While the CAPL-2 was designed for children aged 8-12 years, the use of pictorial items, as proposed by Barnett et al. (2022), could optimise the measurement of these domains. However, the students were accompanied by assessors who were present to answer their questions in case of comprehension difficulties, which may have partially mitigated this limitation.

Third, the CAPL-2 has not been formally validated in French, even though the authors report in their validation paper that it is available for use in both English and French (Longmuir, Gunnell, et al., 2018).

Fourth, the substantial attrition during the analysis of associations between physical literacy profiles and movement behaviour distribution metrics (i.e., from 99 recruited participants to 47 with four or more valid days of accelerometer measurement) resulted in very small sample sizes across the four physical literacy profile categories, with the lowest count for the "Beginning" profile (n = 4). Such small sample sizes are likely to generate estimates that are not robust enough to be useful for planning confirmatory studies. Nevertheless, sensitivity analyses conducted with participants having three or more valid days, and separately two or more valid days, reached a total of 71 participants in both cases. Sample sizes were multiplied by 1.5 to 2 across physical literacy profiles (e.g., n = 8 for the "Beginning" profile), yet results were nearly identical (see sections 5 and 6 from the HTML report of the project's analytical pipeline: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24053778). This suggests that the robustness of our results may not be as low as expected, likely thanks to the rank-based procedures used in our study. Of note, the lower proportion of participants in the "Beginning" profile was expected, as this category consistently shows fewer participants than the two middle categories in the literature (Hadier et al., 2024; Longmuir et al., 2015).

Fifth, the proportion of participants within the "Excelling" profile was relatively high compared to the other profiles. This might be related to the socio-economic and cultural context in which the study has been conducted. Indeed, Avrillé is well known for its active sport policy, and most of its schools have a social index above the national average, meaning that families' socioeconomic and cultural background is conducive to children's learning, including physical activity skills. This imbalance in the distribution of the participants across the physical literacy profiles could be viewed as problematic for interpreting differences between these profiles if other potential confounding variables were related to the physical literacy profiles. In the present case, girls and boys were equally distributed in each physical literacy profile, avoiding its potential influence on physical literacy profile comparisons.

Sixth, the association between intensity gradient and step count, that is used in the CAPL-2 tool, could be considered as not trivial (r = 0.44). Therefore, future studies should consider, where possible, other activity intensity metrics to reduce the risk of circularity when examining associations between physical literacy profile and movement behaviours.

Finally, we were unable to use the accelerometer logbooks that aimed at identifying when accelerometers were removed during waking periods and what activities were performed during those periods. Indeed, several logbooks were either incompletely filled out or lost. The main drawback of this is that we could not assess the representativeness of the measured step count as a reflection of children's actual physical activity profile, particularly in cases where children were required to participate in physical activities during which the devices could not be worn. However, this limitation is shared by the large majority of studies investigating movement behaviour using wearable devices, and is understandable given the difficulty and burden that accurately completing a logbook every day may represent for a child.

CONCLUSION & FUTURE DIRECTIONS

In the present study, boys were more likely to have higher physical literacy scores than girls, particularly for total physical literacy, the motivation and confidence domain, the physical competence domain, the daily behaviour domain, and several components from these domains. Exploratory testing suggests prioritising total physical literacy score and the motivation and confidence domain score as primary targets for future confirmatory studies aiming to establish a possible difference between French girls and boys in a similar sociodemographic and cultural context, even if other physical literacy domains and sets of physical literacy subcomponents could also be good candidates for investigating sex differences.

Our study also identified an interesting association between physical literacy profiles and time spent in activity bins of higher intensity (i.e., the intensity gradient), but less clearly with the pattern of sedentary time accumulation (i.e., the power-law exponent alpha). Exploratory testing suggests targeting primarily the intensity gradient in future studies to confirm the ability of physical literacy profiles to inform the intensity dimension of the physical activity profile concept.

Finally, it is important to emphasise again that the present study is exploratory. Therefore, all effects identified as significant should be interpreted as promising avenues for future research, requiring confirmation in subsequent studies with adequate error control and sufficient statistical power. If confirmed, these results could inform multi-component interventions grounded in physical literacy to reduce sex inequalities in physical literacy and improve movement behaviour profiles, such as the distribution of physical activity intensities and the reduction of prolonged sedentary periods. SOFTWARE

• Initial tasks of the data analysis workflow (import, tidy, and transform data): {tidyverse} (Wickham & RStudio, 2023); {tidyselect} (Henry & Wickham, 2024).

• Figures: {ggplot2} (Wickham, 2016); {Hmisc} (Harell et al., 2026); {patchwork} (Pedersen, 2025); {ggrain} (Judd et al., 2026).

• Tables: {flextable} (Gohel et al., 2026).

• Descriptive statistics: {skimr} (Waring et al., 2026); {gtsummary} (Sjoberg et al., 2021).

• Brunner-Munzel test: {rankFD} (Konietschke et al., 2022).

• Nonparametric multivariate analysis: {npmv} (W. Burchett & Ellis, 2025).

• Principal component analysis: {stats} (R Core Team, 2024); {factoextra} (Kassambara et al., 2026).

• Correlation analysis: {correlation} (Makowski et al., 2025).

• Analytical pipeline implementation: {targets} (W. Landau, 2021), {tarchetypes} (W. M. Landau et al., 2025).

• Package dependencies recording: {groundhog} (Simonsohn et al., 2026).
